stimuli.text: A block of mass 5 kg on a 30° incline is connected by a light string over a light, frictionless pulley at the top of the incline to a hanging block of mass 8 kg. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline is 0.1. The system is released from rest, and the hanging block descends.
A block of mass 0.7 kg on a horizontal frictionless surface is attached to a spring. Its position is $$x(t) = 0.15\cos(2t)$$, with x in meters and t in seconds.
Students measure the period of a simple pendulum for several string lengths, using small amplitudes.
A solid cylinder (I = ½MR²) and a hoop (I = MR²) of equal mass M and radius R are released from rest at the top of the same ramp of height 1.9 m. Both roll without slipping.

questions.stem: A particle's position is $$x(t) = 2t^3 + 4t^2 + 8t$$, with x in meters and t in seconds. What is its acceleration at $$t = 4$$ s?

options.why: Bring each exponent down as a factor when differentiating.
The derivative of 2bt is 2b, which also remains.
Correct. Differentiate twice: a = 6at + 2b.
That is the velocity; differentiate again.

questions.explanation: a(t) = 12t + 8, so at t = 4 the value is 56.

questions.stem: An oscillator's position is $$x(t) = 0.02\cos(3t)$$ m. What is its maximum speed?

options.why: v_max = Aω.
Correct. v_max = Aω.
That is a_max.
Multiply by ω.

questions.stem: A force $$F(x) = 2x^2$$ N acts along the x-axis. How much work does it do on an object moving from $$x = 1$$ m to $$x = 4$$ m?

options.why: Correct. W = ∫F dx.
Integrate; do not just evaluate F.
The force is not constant.
Divide by n + 1 when integrating.

questions.stem: A spring with $$k = 330$$ N/m is compressed 0.09 m and launches a 0.9 kg block across a frictionless surface. What is the block's speed after leaving the spring?

options.why: The ½ appears on both sides.
Correct. ½kx² = ½mv².
Use energy: v = x√(k/m).
Take the square root.

questions.stem: A car rounds a flat curve of radius 110 m. The coefficient of static friction is 0.5. What is the maximum speed without skidding?

options.why: Correct. Static friction supplies the centripetal force: μmg = mv²/r.
Include the friction coefficient.
μ multiplies g r.
Take the square root.

questions.stem: A 0.2 kg ball hits a wall at 11 m/s and rebounds at 9 m/s. The contact lasts 0.1 s. What is the average force from the wall?

options.why: Correct. Δp = m(v_f − v_i) with the direction reversed.
Include the rebound.
Divide by time.
The velocity reverses, so the speeds add.

questions.stem: A 0.9 kg mass oscillates on a spring with $$k = 105$$ N/m. What is the period?

options.why: Include the 2π.
That is the frequency.
The ratio is m/k.
Correct. T = 2π√(m/k).

questions.stem: Two springs with constants 50 N/m and 60 N/m are connected in parallel and support a 1 kg mass at rest. How far do they stretch in total?

options.why: Correct. k_eq = k₁ + k₂.
Both springs share the load.
The force is the weight, mg.
Series and parallel rules are reversed.

questions.stem: A ball rolls off a horizontal ledge 15 m high at 7 m/s. How far from the base of the ledge does it land?

options.why: Fall time is √(2h/g).
Correct. Fall time from the height, times the horizontal speed.
Horizontal and vertical motion are independent.
Take the square root for the time.

questions.stem: A motor lifts a 270 kg load 26 m at constant speed in 6 s. What average power does it deliver?

options.why: That is the work; divide by time.
P = W/t.
Include g.
Correct. P = mgh/t.

questions.stem: A 1 kg cart moving at 9 m/s collides with and sticks to a 5 kg cart at rest. What is their speed after the collision?

options.why: Correct. Momentum is conserved; kinetic energy is not.
The carts share the momentum.
Use m₁v₁ for the initial momentum.
Kinetic energy is not conserved here.

questions.explanation: v_f = 1·9/6 = 1.5 m/s; kinetic energy lost = 33.8 J.

questions.stem: A 58 kg person stands on a scale in an elevator that is accelerating downward at 3 m/s². What does the scale read?

options.why: Check the direction of the acceleration.
Correct. The scale reads the normal force: N − mg = ma (up positive).
The acceleration changes the normal force.
Include gravity.

questions.stem: A uniform 5 m beam weighing 400 N rests on supports at both ends. A 200 N load sits 1 m from the left end. What force does the right support exert?

options.why: That is the left support's force.
Include the beam's weight at its center.
Correct. Take torques about the left support.
The load is not at the center.

questions.stem: A 500 kg car heading east at 14 m/s collides with a 1500 kg car heading north at 10 m/s, and they lock together. What is their speed just after the collision?

options.why: Momentum is a vector; add components at right angles.
Weight each velocity by its mass.
Divide by the total mass.
Correct. Conserve momentum in x and y separately, then combine.

questions.stem: A uniform disk of mass 3 kg and radius 0.2 m spins at 10 rad/s on a frictionless axle. A 1 kg lump of clay is dropped onto the rim and sticks. What is the new angular speed?

options.why: Use rotational inertias, not masses.
The clay's inertia is mR².
Kinetic energy is not conserved in a sticking collision.
Correct. Angular momentum is conserved: I_iω_i = I_fω_f.

questions.stem: An object of mass 0.9 kg falls from rest with a drag force $$F = -bv$$, where $$b = 0.04$$ kg/s. What is the time constant of its approach to terminal speed?

options.why: τ = m/b.
Correct. From m dv/dt = mg − bv, τ = m/b.
τ has units of seconds: m/b.
That is the terminal speed.

questions.explanation: v_T = mg/b = 221 m/s and τ = m/b = 22.5 s.

questions.stem: A uniform rod of length 0.9 m swings about a pivot at one end with small amplitude. What is its period?

options.why: A rod is a physical pendulum, not a simple one.
I = mL²/3.
d is L/2, the distance to the center of mass.
Correct. T = 2π√(I/(mgd)) with I = mL²/3 and d = L/2.

questions.stem: A wheel spinning at 52 rad/s slows uniformly to rest in 7 s. How many revolutions does it make while stopping?

options.why: Recheck the average.
The average angular speed is ω₀/2.
That is in radians; convert to revolutions.
Correct. Δθ = ½ω₀t, then divide by 2π.

questions.stem: Masses of 9 kg and 4 kg hang on either side of a light, frictionless pulley. What is the tension in the string?

options.why: Use T = m₂(g + a).
The lighter mass accelerates up, so T exceeds its weight.
The heavier mass accelerates down, so T is less than its weight.
Correct. T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂).

questions.stem: A block slides down a 20° incline. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.25. What is the magnitude of its acceleration?

options.why: Correct. a = g(sin θ − μk cos θ).
Friction acts up the slope.
The component along the incline is mg sin θ.
Friction depends on the normal force, mg cos θ.

questions.stem: A planet has 0.5 times Earth's mass and 0.5 times Earth's radius. What is the gravitational field strength at its surface? (Earth's is 9.8 N/kg.)

options.why: g depends on 1/R², not 1/R.
The ratio is inverted.
g decreases with radius.
Correct. g ∝ M/R².

questions.stem: A boat points straight across a river 110 m wide, moving at 4 m/s relative to the water. The current flows at 3 m/s. How long does the crossing take?

options.why: Correct. The current does not change the time to cross; it only carries the boat downstream.
The current is perpendicular to the heading.
The perpendicular component alone sets the crossing time.
The current is perpendicular to the heading.

questions.stem: A car moving at 23 m/s brakes with a constant deceleration of 7 m/s². How far does it travel before stopping?

options.why: Divide by 2a, not a.
Δx = v₀²/(2a).
That is the stopping time in seconds.
Correct. Use v² = v₀² + 2aΔx with v = 0.

questions.stem: A uniform disk of mass 6 kg and radius 0.6 m spins at 5 rad/s on a frictionless axle. A 1 kg lump of clay is dropped onto the rim and sticks. What is the new angular speed?

options.why: Kinetic energy is not conserved in a sticking collision.
Use rotational inertias, not masses.
The clay's inertia is mR².
Correct. Angular momentum is conserved: I_iω_i = I_fω_f.

questions.stem: A 3 kg mass hangs from a light string wrapped around a uniform disk pulley of mass 4 kg that turns on a frictionless axle. What is the acceleration of the mass?

options.why: For a disk, I/R² = M/2.
The pulley's inertia reduces the acceleration.
Correct. a = mg/(m + M/2), using I = ½MR² and a = Rα.
I/R² = M/2.

questions.explanation: mg − T = ma and TR = ½MR²(a/R) give a = 5.88 m/s².

questions.stem: The potential energy of a particle is $$U(x) = 2x^3 - 24x$$ J. At what positive x is the particle in stable equilibrium?

options.why: Correct. Equilibrium where dU/dx = 0; stable at a minimum.
Take the square root.
dU/dx = 3ax² − b.
Set the derivative, not U, to zero.

questions.explanation: dU/dx = 6x² − 24 = 0 gives x = 2 m; d²U/dx² > 0 there, so it is stable.

questions.stem: A solid cylinder rolls without slipping from rest down a ramp of height 2.5 m. What is its speed at the bottom?

options.why: Correct. mgh = ½mv²(1 + β) with I = ½MR².
Some energy goes into rotation.
Rotational energy is ½Iω² = ½βmv².
That is only correct for a hoop.

questions.stem: A uniform disk of mass 3 kg and radius 0.5 m rotates about an axis perpendicular to it, 0.5 m from its center. What is its rotational inertia?

options.why: Include the disk's own I about its center.
Correct. Parallel-axis theorem: I = ½MR² + Md².
The axis is not through the center.
The parallel-axis term is Md².

questions.stem: A uniform rod of length 0.7 m is pivoted at one end and released from rest in a horizontal position. What is its angular acceleration just after release?

options.why: Correct. τ = Mg(L/2) and I = ML²/3 give α = 3g/(2L).
Use τ = Iα with I = ML²/3.
τ = MgL/2.
The weight acts at L/2.

questions.stem: A planet has mass $$8 \times 10^{23}$$ kg and radius $$8 \times 10^{7}$$ m. What is the escape speed from its surface? ($$G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$$ N·m²/kg²)

options.why: Correct. ½mv² = GMm/R.
That is the circular orbit speed; escape needs √2 times more.
Take the square root.
Potential energy uses 1/R.

questions.stem: The potential energy of a particle is $$U(x) = 3x^3 - 6x$$ J. At what positive x is the particle in stable equilibrium?

options.why: Set the derivative, not U, to zero.
Correct. Equilibrium where dU/dx = 0; stable at a minimum.
Take the square root.
dU/dx = 3ax² − b.

questions.explanation: dU/dx = 9x² − 6 = 0 gives x = 0.816 m; d²U/dx² > 0 there, so it is stable.

questions.stem: A 1 kg ball on a 1.2 m string moves in a vertical circle. At the bottom of the circle its speed is 6 m/s. What is the tension in the string there?

options.why: Centripetal force uses v².
Correct. At the bottom, T − mg = mv²/r.
Check the direction of gravity relative to the center.
Include gravity.

questions.stem: A 6 kg object at rest experiences a net force $$F(t) = 10t^2$$ N from $$t = 0$$ to $$t = 2$$ s. What is its final speed?

options.why: Correct. Impulse ∫F dt equals the change in momentum.
Divide by the mass to get speed.
The force is not constant.
Integrate the force over time.

questions.stem: A ball is launched from level ground at 15 m/s at 70° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, what is its horizontal range?

options.why: Correct. Treat horizontal and vertical motion separately.
Range uses sin 2θ.
Use the full time of flight.
That is the maximum range, at 45°.

questions.explanation: v₀x = 5.13 m/s, v₀y = 14.1 m/s. R = v₀² sin 2θ/g = 14.8 m.

questions.stem: A 1 kg ball moving at +4 m/s collides elastically head-on with a 4 kg ball at rest. What is the velocity of the 4 kg ball afterward (positive in the original direction)?

options.why: Only equal masses exchange velocities.
Correct. Elastic: conserve momentum and kinetic energy (relative velocity reverses).
Kinetic energy is conserved too.
That would be a sticking collision.

questions.explanation: v₁' = (m₁ − m₂)v/(m₁ + m₂) = -2.4 m/s; v₂' = 2m₁v/(m₁ + m₂) = 1.6 m/s.

questions.stem: A mass on a spring oscillates with angular frequency 11 rad/s and amplitude 0.16 m. What is its speed when it is 0.016 m from equilibrium?

options.why: Correct. v = ω√(A² − x²), from conservation of energy.
Speed is greatest at equilibrium, not at the ends.
Use A² − x² under a square root.
That is the maximum speed, at x = 0.

questions.stem: A constant torque of 6 N·m acts on a wheel ($$I = 1.5$$ kg·m²) initially at rest, through 2 revolutions. What is the wheel's final angular speed?

options.why: Convert revolutions to radians.
½Iω² = W; solve for ω.
Correct. Work τΔθ (in radians) equals ½Iω².
W = ½Iω².

questions.stem: A block starts from rest and slides 3 m down a 45° incline with coefficient of kinetic friction 0.3. What is its speed at the bottom?

options.why: Use the vertical drop, L sin θ.
Correct. mgh − μmg cos θ·L = ½mv².
Friction depends on the normal force, mg cos θ.
Friction removes energy.

questions.stem: A rod lies along the x-axis from $$x = 0$$ to $$x = 1$$ m and has linear mass density $$\lambda = kx^2$$. Where is its center of mass?

options.why: Integrate x·xⁿ and xⁿ correctly.
The rod is not uniform.
The exponents are n + 2 and n + 1.
Correct. x_cm = ∫xλ dx / ∫λ dx.

questions.stem: A 25 g bullet moving at 470 m/s embeds in a 2.8 kg block hanging from strings. How high does the block rise?

options.why: Find the block's speed after the collision first.
Kinetic energy is not conserved in the collision.
Correct. Momentum for the collision, then energy for the swing.
h = V²/(2g).

questions.explanation: V = 4.16 m/s after the collision; h = V²/(2g) = 0.883 m.

questions.title: Block on an incline with a hanging mass

parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a free-body diagram for the 5 kg block, labeling each force.

rubric.criterion: Weight down, normal force perpendicular to the incline, tension up the incline.
Kinetic friction down the incline (opposite the motion).

parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the acceleration of the system in terms of the masses, θ, μ and g, then calculate its value.

rubric.criterion: Newton's second law applied to each block (or the system).

parts.prompt: Calculate the tension in the string.
Calculate the speed of the blocks after the hanging block has descended 1 m, and the work done by friction on the incline block during that motion.

rubric.criterion: Work by friction, with a negative sign.

parts.prompt: Sketch (describe) graphs of position, velocity and acceleration versus time for one period, aligned vertically.

rubric.criterion: Position is a cosine starting at +A; velocity is a negative sine starting at 0.
rubric.example: x starts at 0.15 m; v starts at 0 and goes negative.

rubric.criterion: Acceleration starts at its negative maximum and is opposite in sign to position throughout.

parts.prompt: Derive expressions for v(t) and a(t), and determine the maximum speed and maximum acceleration.
Calculate the spring constant and the period.
Calculate the total mechanical energy and describe how kinetic and potential energy vary during one period.

rubric.example: K is maximum at x = 0 and zero at x = ±A; U is the reverse; the sum is constant. Each varies twice per period.

parts.prompt: Describe a procedure the students could use to measure the period accurately, including how to reduce uncertainty.

rubric.example: Time 10 swings with a stopwatch and divide by 10.

rubric.criterion: Keep the amplitude small and repeat trials.
rubric.example: Release from under about 10° and average several trials.

parts.prompt: Identify quantities to graph that would give a straight line, and explain how g can be found from the graph.
Plot (describe) the linearized data and draw a best-fit line. Use it to calculate an experimental value of g.
The students repeat the experiment with a much larger amplitude. Predict how the measured periods would change and explain.

rubric.criterion: Periods increase slightly; the small-angle approximation (sin θ ≈ θ) no longer holds.
rubric.example: The restoring torque is less than proportional to θ at large angles.

parts.prompt: Without calculating, predict which object reaches the bottom first. Justify your prediction using energy.

rubric.example: It has the smaller rotational inertia per MR².

rubric.criterion: Justification: less of its energy goes into rotation, so more is translational kinetic energy.

parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the speed at the bottom of an object with rotational inertia βMR², in terms of g, h and β.

rubric.criterion: Energy conservation including both forms of kinetic energy, with v = Rω.

parts.prompt: Calculate the speed of each object at the bottom.
Explain whether your derived expression is consistent with your prediction in part (a), and why neither speed depends on M or R.

rubric.criterion: Smaller β gives larger v, consistent with the prediction.
M and R cancel in the energy equation.
rubric.example: Only the shape factor β matters.
